# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–27 (Complete – Updated 196)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Autumn in continental Europe, seventh year after Waterloo**. John Sedley deceased (died peacefully in sleep; buried at Brompton churchyard beside wife). Mr. Osborne deceased (died four days after stroke; found at foot of dressing-table). Major Dobbin appointed executor of Osborne's will. Rawdon governs Coventry Island. Georgy established as heir. **Continental tour progressing**: Amelia, Georgy, Jos, and Major Dobbin on steamship and carriage tour; landed Rotterdam, traveled to Cologne, now established in Pumpernickel (a small German principality) for autumn/winter season. **Year noted as 1830 (French Revolution occurred this year)**.
- **Major locations**: London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Gaunt House, Regent Club, Knightsbridge Barracks, Russell Square, Brompton, Conduit Street, Hart Street Bloomsbury, Southampton Row, Kensington Gardens, Camberwell, Slaughters' Inn, Haymarket Theatre, Gillespie Street); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate; Piccadilly; Madras; St. Helena; Cape; Southampton; Staveton; Belgium (Brussels, Mount St. John, Waterloo, Laeken); Bengal; Salford; Regent's Park; Richmond (Star and Garter); Gulton; Harrowgate; Hill farms; Roehampton; Hampton Court; Calcutta; Jamaica; Rotterdam; Cologne; Free City of Judenstadt; Rhine region; Rhineland; **Pumpernickel** (small German principality with Court, theatre, Duke's schloss, Prime Minister's lodgings, Aurelius Platz, Zwieback's Conditorey, Saint Michael's Fountain, Artillery Place, Stadthaus, Town Hall, Redoute, gardens with Trophonius' cave, nymphbath, Niagara cataract); Mirecombe; Dunholt; Dunwick; Quenwick; Humbourg-Schlippenschloppen; Ems; Aix-la-Chapelle; Baden-Baden; Salwick; Elephant (lodging-house); Boulogne; Dieppe; Portman Square; Brussels; Paris; Wildbad; Strasburg; St. Petersburg; Toplitz; Vienna; Pincian Hill (Rome); Naples; Castle Gaunt; Trinity House; White Friars.

## John Sedley's Final Illness and Death (Chapter 26)
Amelia nursed father devotedly during final illness. Old Sedley forgave past grievances. Died peacefully in sleep. Buried at Brompton churchyard beside wife. Major Dobbin, Jos, and Georgy followed remains to grave.

## Mr. Osborne's Stroke and Death (Chapter 26)
Osborne found in dressing-room at foot of dressing-table in fit. Pocket contained letter from George written from Waterloo and key to box of papers with broken seals—likely read night before seizure. Died in four days without speaking again.

**Will Terms**: Half property left to George Osborne (minor); remainder between two sisters. Mr. Bullock to continue commercial house. **Annuity**: Five hundred pounds to Amelia, "the widow of my beloved son, George Osborne," who resumed guardianship of boy. Major William Dobbin appointed executor, left sum "sufficient to purchase his commission as a Lieutenant-Colonel, or to be disposed of in any way he may think fit." Will showed "the hatred which he had so long cherished had gone out of his heart."

## Amelia's Transformation (Chapter 26)
Upon learning of William's bounty, Amelia "sank on her knees, and prayed for blessings on that constant and kind heart." During continental tour, discovered Dobbin's true gentlemanly character and generous heart. "Emmy, in this happy time, found that hers underwent a very great change in respect of the merits of the Major."

## Continental Tour (Chapter 26)
Party landed Rotterdam, traveled by steamer to Cologne. Jos announced arrival as "Herr Graf Lord von Sedley nebst Begleitung aus London," insisted on court dress, announced intention to be presented at foreign courts. Amelia drew constantly, sat upon steamers' decks, sketched crags and castles, mounted donkeys to ascend towers attended by Georgy and Dobbin. "Perhaps it was the happiest time of both their lives...this couple were very decently contented, and enjoyed as pleasant a summer tour as any pair that left England that year."

## Pumpernickel Arrival and Society (Chapter 26–27)
**Theatre and British Recognition**: Party attended theatre. Tapeworm, Charge d'Affaires (nephew and heir of old Marshal Tiptoff, now deceased), rose in his box and bowed. Near performance end, Tapeworm approached Jos with invitation to stay. Jos committed to autumn in Pumpernickel after Doctor von Glauber convinced him mineral springs would "infallibly restore the Bengalee to youth and slimness." Next day, Tapeworm presented Jos and Major to Victor Aurelius XVII. Straightway invited to dinner at Court. Upon announcement of intention to stay, "politest ladies of the whole town instantly called upon Mrs. Osborne"; as not one was under rank of Baroness, "Jos's delight was beyond expression."

**Emmy at Court and Evening Dress**: Emmy presented to august family. On certain days mourning not admitted at Court, so she appeared in pink crape dress with diamond ornament. "She looked so pretty in this costume that the Duke and Court (putting out of the question the Major, who had scarcely ever seen her before in an evening dress, and vowed that she did not look five-and-twenty) all admired her excessively."

**Emmy's Social Activities (Chapter 27)**: Before winter far advanced, Emmy received company with great propriety and modesty. Had French master, received singing lessons from Madam Strumpff. German ladies fell in love with her. Major made himself Georgy's tutor; they rode out evenings by side of Emmy's carriage. Drove about with German friends; Jos asleep on back-seat of barouche.

**Jos's Romantic Interest**: Jos becoming sweet upon Grafinn Fanny de Butterbrod, gentle tender-hearted young creature, a Canoness and Countess with scarcely ten pounds per year. Fanny declared being Amelia's sister "greatest delight Heaven could bestow."

## Georgy Osborne (Chapter 26–27)
Now eleven years old. Day boy at Reverend Lawrence Veal's School (Hart Street, Bloomsbury). Marked aristos in Greek, optimus in Latin, très bien in French. Boy's "quick brain" revealed grandfather "a dullard." Now heir to half Osborne's substantial property. Remained active, imperious, good-natured. **At Gambling (Chapter 27)**: With relations away at Court festival, Georgy came to Stadthaus Ball with uncle's courier Kirsch, hankered round roulette and trente-et-quarante tables. Major Dobbin instantly pulled him back from temptation, showed him eloquently why he shouldn't be there, housed him, went to bed.

## Rebecca's Degradation and Continued Wanderings (Chapter 27)

**Moral Decline**: "This abattement and degradation did not take place all at once; it was brought about by degrees, after her calamity, and after many struggles to keep up." Lingered in London while Rawdon prepared for departure to Coventry Island. Made attempts to see Sir Pitt Crawley but never succeeded; Lady Jane interposed.

**Boulogne Refuge**: Perched upon French coast at Boulogne. Lived in genteel, widowed manner. Received notice to quit from landlord—told she was "quite an unfit person to have at his hotel, where English ladies would not sit down with her."

**Attempted Respectability**: Went to church regularly, took up cause of widows of shipwrecked fishermen, subscribed to Assembly and WOULDN'T waltz. "She did everything that was respectable, and that is why we dwell upon this part of her career with more fondness than upon subsequent parts of her history, which are not so pleasant."

**Mrs. Hook Eagles and Dieppe**: Mrs. Hook Eagles took her up at Dieppe—a woman without blemish. Pronounced Mrs. Crawley an angel, her husband a ruffian, Lord Steyne an unprincipled wretch. Becky respectable and orderly at first, but life of humdrum virtue grew tedious before long. Young Mr. Eagles came from Cambridge; his mother, seeing impression Becky made, gave her warning.

**Brussels Gambling and Degradation**: At Brussels, recommended to Madame la Comtesse de Borodino's table d'hote and ecarte table. Played audaciously—first for little, then escalating: five-franc pieces, Napoleons, notes, ten sous. Borrowed from young gentlemen. When Becky left Brussels, owed three months' pension. Countess de Borodino informs every English visitor that "Madame Rawdon was no better than a vipere."

**Wanderings and Bohemian Life**: "So our little wanderer went about setting up her tent in various cities of Europe, as restless as Ulysses or Bampfylde Moore Carew." Vagabond upon earth—when got money, gambled; when gambled it away, put to shifts to live. **RUMOR/CLAIM**: Said once seen at St. Petersburg but summarily dismissed by police. **RUMOR/CLAIM**: Found maternal grandmother at Paris—not a Montmorenci but "a hideous old box-opener at a theatre on the Boulevards." **RUMOR/CLAIM**: When particularly down on luck, gave concerts and lessons. Madame de Raudon had matinee musicale at Wildbad with Herr Spoff. **RUMOR/CLAIM**: Mr. Eaves declared he was at Strasburg in 1830 when Madame Rebecque appeared in opera of Dame Blanche, hissed off stage.

**Brussels Recollections**: Looked up at little entresol she had occupied at Brussels, thought of Bareacres family. Went to Waterloo and Laeken, where George Osborne's monument struck her. Made little sketch. "That poor Cupid!" she said; "how dreadfully he was in love with me, and what a fool he was! I wonder whether little Emmy is alive."

## Rebecca at Pumpernickel—Encounter with Jos (Chapter 27)
At Stadthaus gambling, Jos remained behind over play-table. Woman asked him to give good luck in foreign accent with pretty French accent. Revealed herself as **Rebecca (Madame de Raudon)**, formerly involved with Rawdon Crawley. Spoke of seeing "dear Amelia" that day, noted she "looked pretty and happy." Mentioned Jos's changes, lamented her own unhappiness.

**Encounter with Lord Steyne and Flight from Rome**: Later in Rome, Rebecca encountered Lord Steyne at Pincian Hill. Met Monsieur Fiche, Steyne's confidential man, who followed her from hotel with warning: "I have some advice to give Madame." Fiche warned her Steyne was enraged when he saw her—"He was like a madman last night when he came home." Madame de Belladonna (Steyne's companion) "made him a scene about you and fired off in one of her furies." Fiche told her: "You did wrong to show yourself to him. And if you stay here you will repent it." Rushed her down alley as Lord Steyne's barouche came whirling along avenue, bearing Madame de Belladonna lolling on cushions with King Charles, and "old Steyne stretched at her side with a livid face and ghastly eyes...ordinarily, they gave no light, and seemed tired of looking out on a world of which almost all the pleasure and all the best beauty had palled upon the worn-out wicked old man."

**Whether Steyne Intended Murder**: "Whether my lord really had murderous intentions towards Mrs. Becky as Monsieur Fiche said...or whether he simply had a commission to frighten Mrs. Crawley out of a city where his Lordship proposed to pass the winter...is a point which has never been ascertained: but the threat had its effect upon the little woman, and she sought no more to intrude herself upon the presence of her old patron."

## Lord Steyne's Death (Chapter 27)
**Melancholy End**: Befell at Naples two months after French Revolution of 1830. "Most Honourable George Gustavus, Marquis of Steyne, Earl of Gaunt and of Gaunt Castle, in the Peerage of Ireland, Viscount Hellborough, Baron Pitchley and Grillsby...died after a series of fits brought on, as the papers said, by the shock occasioned to his lordship's sensibilities by the downfall of the ancient French monarchy."

**Obituary and Legacy**: "An eloquent catalogue appeared in a weekly print, describing his virtues, his magnificence, his talents, and his good actions." His body buried at Naples; heart "brought back to Castle Gaunt in a silver urn." Mr. Wagg eulogized: "In him...the poor and the Fine Arts have lost a beneficent patron, society one of its most brilliant ornaments, and England one of her loftiest patriots and statesmen."

**Will Disputed**: Attempt made to force "Jew's-eye" diamond from Madame de Belladonna. Monsieur Fiche proved ring presented to Madame de Belladonna two days before Marquis's death, as were bank-notes, jewels, Neapolitan and French bonds found in secretaire. **Since Steyne's death, Fiche returned to native country, now respected and purchased from his Prince the title of Baron Ficci**.

## Rebecca's Present Happiness at Pumpernickel (Chapter 27)
"Becky liked the life. She was at home with everybody in the place, pedlars, punters, tumblers, students and all. She was of a wild, roving nature, inherited from father and mother, who were both Bohemians, by taste and circumstance." "How pleasant was all the bustle to her now that her purse was full of the money which little Georgy had won for her the night before!"

## Rawdon Crawley (Chapter 23–24, 27)
Governor of Coventry Island, three thousand per year. Complete moral transformation. Separated from Rebecca permanently after duel with Steyne. Financial settlement: pays her three hundred pounds per year on undertaking she would never trouble him.

## Other Reconciliations (Chapter 26)
Mrs. Frederick Bullock reconciled to Amelia and Georgy. Bullock family made irruption into Amelia's garden. Miss Swartz and husband came thundering from Hampton Court with flaming yellow liveries, "as impetuously fond of Amelia as ever."
